facts.statement: The Earth and Moon are slowly drifting apart at the rate that fingernails grow, 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) per year.

source.title: Laser Beams Reflected Between Earth and Moon Boost Science

facts.statement: Reflectors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts (Apollo 14's panel has 100 corner-cube mirrors) return laser light in about 2.5 seconds on average, giving the Earth–Moon distance to within a few millimetres.

source.title: Laser Beams Reflected Between Earth and Moon Boost Science

facts.statement: From Apollo 14's reflector placement in 1971 to 2026 (55 years) at 3.8 cm per year, the Moon has moved about 209 cm, about 2 metres, farther away.

The energy propelling the Moon away comes primarily from Earth's oceans, which bulge out in response to the Moon's gravity and exert a gravitational pull of their own on the Moon; its drift slows as it goes.
Once the Moon has drifted 14,600 miles (23,500 km) farther out, it will appear too small from Earth to cover the Sun; that is another 600-million-plus years away.
Photo of the total solar eclipse of 21 August 2017.
